The reproductive biology of the Two-spot swimming crab, Charybdis bimaculata, has been characterized through detailed laboratory observations of ovigerous females. Embryonic development proceeds within a brood mass carried externally on the pleopods, with pigmented eyed eggs measuring approximately 0.031 cm [Lb = approximately 0.031 cm] in diameter. Interestingly, non-pigmented eyed eggs were observed to be slightly smaller at 0.028 cm diameter, a difference likely reflecting the stage of yolk utilization and eye pigment deposition during organogenesis. Based on the spherical shape of these eggs and assuming a density of 1 g/cm³, the calculated wet weight at birth for a newly hatched larva is 1.56 × 10⁻⁵ g [Wwb = 1.56 × 10⁻⁵ g], a remarkably diminutive mass that underscores the planktonic existence of the early zoeal stages. This initial size is critical for understanding subsequent larval dispersal and susceptibility to predation in the water column.

As individuals progress through successive molts, the onset of sexual maturation is demarcated by a distinct pubertal molt. For female C. bimaculata, the carapace length at which this pubertal molt occurs has been established at 1.183 cm [Lp = 1.183 cm], a size that signals the transition to a reproductively active adult capable of mating and egg production. Males undergo this developmental milestone at a slightly larger carapace length of 1.25 cm [Lp = 1.25 cm], a difference partly attributed to the energetic demands of gamete production and competition for access to receptive females. The timing of these pubertal events is tightly linked to environmental temperature regimes.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 438 days [am = approximately 438 days], a figure derived from systematic cohort studies. The complete life cycle, from larval hatching through natural death, typically spans approximately 438 days [am = approximately 438 days] under these thermal conditions at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 1.2 years, places C. bimaculata among the shorter-lived members of the Portunidae family, a life-history strategy that is often correlated with rapid growth, early maturation, and high fecundity—a pattern consistent with an r-selected reproductive strategy typical of many portunid crabs inhabiting variable coastal environments.

Comparative analyses of growth trajectories reveal that female crabs experience a period of rapid size increase following the pubertal molt, eventually reaching a larger asymptotic carapace width than males of equivalent age. The carapace length at puberty for females of 1.183 cm [Lp = 1.183 cm] represents a critical threshold beyond which energy allocation shifts predominantly toward ovarian development and successive brood production. Field surveys have corroborated laboratory findings, demonstrating that the majority of ovigerous females captured in temperate waters possess carapace lengths exceeding this pubertal value, confirming its biological relevance. In contrast, males reach their pubertal molt at a carapace length of 1.25 cm [Lp = 1.25 cm], often achieving this milestone later in the breeding season, a delay that may influence their mating opportunities and reproductive success.

Ecological implications of these life-history parameters are significant for understanding population dynamics and fisheries management. The exceptionally low birth mass of 1.56 × 10⁻⁵ g [Wwb = 1.56 × 10⁻⁵ g] implies an extreme reliance on planktonic food resources during the vulnerable zoeal stages, where high mortality rates are typical—a pattern common among portunid larvae. Furthermore, the maximum lifespan of approximately 438 days [am = approximately 438 days] under stable thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] suggests that C. bimaculata populations can undergo rapid turnover, with multiple generations potentially occurring within a single year in warmer climates. The consistency of the pubertal carapace lengths across different geographic regions points to a genetically canalized developmental program, though slight variations can arise from local thermal regimes or food availability. These combined data provide a robust foundation for future modeling of population resilience.
